rotation.why: A legume after paddy fixes nitrogen in your soil and needs little irrigation. Your soil organic carbon is on the lower side, and pulses improve it while giving a second income.
Grow dhaincha for 45–50 days and plough it in at flowering. It adds 60–80 kg nitrogen per hectare and builds soil structure before the next paddy crop — cutting your urea need.
Return to paddy on improved soil. A short-duration variety lowers water use and leaves time for the rabi pulse. Practise alternate wetting and drying to save about 25% water.

regenerative_plan: Retain paddy stubble after harvest instead of burning — zero-till the rabi pulse directly into it.
Keep living roots in the soil year-round with this rotation to raise soil organic carbon.
Plant Gliricidia on field bunds for green leaf manure over the coming seasons.
soil_note: Your soil pH is close to neutral, which suits both paddy and pulses. Organic carbon is below the ideal level — the green manure season is the fastest way to raise it. Confirm fertiliser doses for the pulse crop with your local KVK after a soil test.
confidence_note: Based on your soil, climate outlook and ICAR regenerative farming guidance. Local market prices and water availability should also guide the final choice — discuss with your KVK.
